**`(profile, id)` is the primary key.** Under amendment ID-RULE-004-A1 an artefact identifier is unique *within its profile*, and two records of different profiles may legitimately carry the same identifier string. So this record is uniquely named by the pair `(synthetic_reference, FB2-SAF-VOC-000001)`, never by `FB2-SAF-VOC-000001` alone. If you are comparing this packet against a reference that gives only the id, it is ambiguous until the profile is also given.

 "identifier_vocabulary": {
  "artefact_identifier": "The string in the `id` field: the pattern FB2-<DOMAIN>-<TYPE>-<NNNNNN>, per the corpus policy's id_scheme. Since amendment ID-RULE-004-A1 (2026-10-04) it is NOT the key of a record: the key is the PAIR (profile, id). 39 identifier strings are carried by two records, one in each profile, and from FB2-VER-EXE-000004 onwards the two records are about different subjects entirely. Under the amended rule that sharing is conformant and no rename is required or permitted, but the id alone still does not resolve, so every reference and every lookup carries or infers a profile.",
  "why_it_is_a_vocabulary_problem": "Three distinct failures follow, and each one produces a wrong answer rather than a missing one. (1) An unqualified identifier reference is ambiguous: FB2-SAF-SGO-000001 names two safety goals whose safe states and degraded states differ. (2) An identifier can be rebound: FB2-VER-EXE-000005 is the contactor-driver host run in one profile and the AFE-communication fixture in the other, so 'FB2-VER-EXE-000005' does not even name a stable subject. (3) RESOLVED 2026-10-04, formerly open and now closed: this failure was that the corpus policy stated that identifiers must be globally unique across profiles and the corpus did not satisfy it, so a reader who trusted the policy over the data would look for a record that did not exist. Amendment ID-RULE-004-A1 in corpus-policy.json amends the rule to per-profile uniqueness, which is what the corpus already did and what the tool already enforced, so the policy and the data now agree and (3) is no longer a failure. Failures (1) and (2) are NOT resolved and are the reason this term remains a vocabulary problem: the validator resolves (profile, id) and so is blind to both, and the only thing that resolves an unqualified reference is the convention stated below.",

  "adopted_convention": "Resolve an identifier as the PAIR (profile, id), never as the id alone. This is now the corpus's primary key by policy, not only by tool behaviour: amendment ID-RULE-004-A1 (2026-10-04) states that an artefact identifier is unique within its profile. Where a record is quoted without its profile, read it as the synthetic_reference copy - that is the copy every safety concept derives from and the copy every safety argument in this corpus is made against. Prefer a field that states the profile, as `profile_basis` does on the as_is functional safety requirements, over inferring it from the directory a record happens to sit in. ON THE 39 SHARED IDENTIFIERS: no rename is required and none is permitted. They were never blocked by ID-RULE-001. An earlier revision of this field said 'Do not renumber: the policy forbids renumbering established identifiers, and 39 of them are shared, so a rename is not available as a repair', which cited ID-RULE-001 and read as though a rename were unavailable in principle. It was not: it was declined on the separate and better evidence recorded at identifier_vocabulary.migration_decision_2026_10_03, namely that renaming inverts this very convention and makes roughly nine hundred unqualified references confidently wrong with no validator able to detect it. Under the amended rule the 39 are conformant, so the question of renaming them is closed rather than deferred. The full list of shared identifiers, and the point at which the rebound identifiers stop naming a stable subject, are recorded in `limitations`.",
  "per_identifier_determination": {
   "how_this_was_determined": "Enumerated every corpus record, grouped its `id` field by value, and compared the two records carrying each shared string. The deciding evidence is mechanical rather than interpretive and it is the same for all thirty-nine: the `origin` field of the two records never agrees. Fourteen as_is records carry origin 'derived' and twenty-five carry 'source_observed'; all thirty-nine synthetic_reference counterparts carry origin 'synthetic'. A record whose origin is source_observed or derived reports the pinned foxBMS sources at commit 308028fb, and a record whose origin is synthetic reports a fictional reference project. No record can be both. Therefore not one of the thirty-nine pairs is a duplicate of a single subject: there are zero duplicates and thirty-nine pairs of distinct subjects sharing one identifier. Three secondary signals corroborate without deciding anything. 16 pairs share a filename and 23 share a title - 16 share both, and every one of the 39 is listed individually in the table below - which is why the collision is easy to miss on inspection: the labels are parallel because the two profiles were authored as a matched pair, not because the two records describe one thing. The label divergence was measured per pair rather than assumed, and the two signals do not start at the same place. Titles diverge earliest, at FB2-VER-EXE-000001, and every execution and test pair from FB2-VER-EXE-000001 onward carries a different title: the as_is copy of EXE-000001 is a real macOS host run of production code and the synthetic_reference copy of the same identifier is a synthetic_fixture. Filenames still coincide for EXE-000001 through EXE-000003 and diverge from FB2-VER-EXE-000004 onward, which is the point at which the identifier stops even naming the same kind of thing. The rebound spans two namespaces: FB2-VER-TMS-000004 pairs the as_is LTC 6813-1 driver communication test against a synthetic independent-monitor test, the same pairing as EXE-000004, and FB2-VER-TMS-000005 pairs the contactor-driver test against the AFE-communication test, the same pairing as EXE-000005. Seven pairs share a filename but not a title - the three FB2-SW-IMP records, EXE-000001 to 000003 and TMS-000002 - which is the signature of the two profiles having been authored as a matched pair whose filenames were kept aligned while the content diverged.",
   "records_checked": 39,
   "duplicate_pairs_same_subject": 0,
   "different_subject_pairs": 39,
   "why_no_pair_is_a_duplicate": "A duplicate would be two records asserting the same thing about the same subject, in which case one of them could be withdrawn and every reference would survive pointed at the survivor. That is not the case here. The clearest worked example is FB2-SAF-FSR-000001, which shares its filename and its title across the two profiles while its fault_reaction differs in substance: the synthetic_reference copy records a latched FAULT mode entered within a 3 ms budget, and the as_is copy records that a measurement failure carrying DIAG severity WARNING does not open the contactors while a DIAG_FATAL_ERROR entry does, at src/app/engine/config/diag_cfg.c:180 and diag_cfg.c:159-162, with the aggregation path through BMS_IsAnyFatalErrorFlagSet() at bms.c:515-531.    "resolution_performed": "NONE, deliberately, and the reason is a boundary and not a preference. Re-issuing either side of thirty-nine identifiers is the policy-sanctioned route - ID-RULE-003 requires supersession and migration to be defined, so a deliberate migration is available and is the right instrument here - but the identifiers are named outside the boundary this pass owns. docs/artifacts/README.md, which this pass may not edit, names seven of them: FB2-SAF-HAZ-000001, FB2-SAF-SGO-000001, FB2-VER-EXE-000001, FB2-VER-EXE-000006, FB2-VER-EXE-000008, FB2-VER-EXE-000012 and FB2-VER-EXE-000015, two of them inside prose ranges written as 'FB2-VER-EXE-000008...000012' and 'FB2-VER-EXE-000001...000006', and one of those sentences already qualifies the range with the words '(profile synthetic_reference)'. test_schemas.py at the repository root names four more. The generated directories docs/artifacts/views and docs/artifacts/spec-documents carry 124 and 157 further occurrences and are produced by two renderers this pass may not edit, so their content cannot be brought back into agreement with a renamed corpus. A rename performed now would leave a committed document, a root-level test and two generated trees asserting identifiers that no longer exist. That is a larger and less honest change than the ambiguity it would settle, so the re-issue is left undone and specified instead.",
   "what_a_migration_must_touch": "Recorded so the migration is a checklist rather than a second investigation. Within the corpus and its registries: the 39 records' own `id` fields, with a supersession entry naming the retired identifier and the new one and the date and author of the move, per ID-RULE-003; every link endpoint in docs/artifacts/traceability/link-registry/ that names one of the 39, in both the source and the target slot and in the `provenance_repair.endpoint_revision_refreshes` history of each; every reviewed_ids entry and every digest_corrections entry in the review records under docs/artifacts/reviews/ that names one of the 39; every standards_mapping backing_artifact and every coverage-plan entry; and every `dependent_records` list in this record. Outside the corpus boundary and therefore not available to this pass: docs/artifacts/README.md, test_schemas.py, the generated views and spec-documents trees, and the graphify-out and graft indexes at the repository root, which hold 195 and 13 occurrences respectively and are caches rather than records. A migration owner needs those four in scope, or needs to accept that the identifiers they name go stale.",
   "which_side_should_move": "The as_is side, if either does, and the reason is referential load rather than preference. The as_is records are the corpus's evidence-bearing profile: they are the ones whose content is anchored to the pinned source at commit 308028fb, they are the copies a reader checking a claim about the real product would land on, and the as_is functional safety requirements already carry `fault_reaction.profile_basis = \"as_is\"` as the corpus's own de facto profile marker. Renumbering the synthetic_reference side leaves the pinned-product account on its established identifiers and moves only the fictional project. That is a recommendation for the migration owner, not an action taken here, and it is contingent on the four out-of-boundary surfaces above being in scope.",
   "invariant_this_pass_preserved": "No record was renumbered, merged, withdrawn or superseded. All thirty-nine identifiers are exactly as they stood at revision 1 of this record. The corpus-wide invariant (profile, id) -> one record still holds, and so does id -> at most two records, one per profile. Both invariants were true before this pass and both are true after it. What is new is that the second is now documented with the evidence that it is a policy violation rather than a coincidence, and with the cost of repairing it."
  },

   "decision": "DECIDED, NOT MIGRATED, and no longer referred. The 39 identifier strings are unchanged. This entry originally recorded the decision as referred to a governance forum; that referral is now answered. Every field below is preserved as it was written on 2026-10-03 because the evidence it contains is the evidence the decision was taken on, and each is annotated where the amendment changes what it means.",
   "instrument_considered": "ID-RULE-003, which requires supersession, deletion and migration to be defined, and is the policy-sanctioned route for exactly this repair.",
   "barriers_that_were_cleared_first": "A previous pass declined the re-issue on a boundary and named four things outside it. Three of the four are no longer outside it and were cleared before this decision was taken. (1) docs/artifacts/README.md, which named seven of the thirty-nine in prose ranges, is editable and its figures have been re-measured. (2) The generated trees docs/artifacts/views and docs/artifacts/spec-documents, which carried 124 and 157 occurrences, are produced by two renderers that are editable and are regenerated from the corpus, so they follow the corpus automatically. (3) test_schemas.py at the repository root, named as a blocker because it names four of the identifiers, is NOT a blocker on inspection: it constructs one self-contained literal sample payload and validates it against requirement.schema.json. It never reads the corpus, never resolves an identifier against the index and asserts nothing about any corpus record, so renaming corpus identifiers cannot affect it. That claimed blocker was void. (4) The remaining out-of-scope references are 465 occurrences in graphify-out/**, which is a generated graph-tool cache and index rather than a corpus record, and 6 in openspec/**, of which four already quote the superseded revision-1 text of SCN-MUT-001's expected finding and are stale independently of any rename.",
   "why_the_migration_was_still_not_performed": "Because renaming either side silently inverts a load-bearing convention and produces wrong answers that no validator can detect. The corpus's own adopted convention, stated in this record at identifier_vocabulary.adopted_convention and at the safe_state and safety goal entries, is that an identifier quoted without its profile is read as the synthetic_reference copy - 'the copy every safety concept derives from and the copy every safety argument in this corpus is made against'. About nine hundred prose references across the record layer rely on that convention, and they are not machine-decidable: a free-text sentence carries no profile. Renaming the synthetic_reference side would therefore not make those sentences correct, it would make them resolve to the as_is copy while continuing to read as though they meant the synthetic one, and no rule would fire, because every renamed identifier would still resolve to exactly one live record. The defect being fixed is 'an unqualified reference is ambiguous, giving the reader two live candidates'. The migration would replace that with 'an unqualified reference is confidently wrong', which is a worse failure, not a better one.",
   "worked_counterexample": "FB2-SAF-TSC-000001 is the synthetic_reference technical safety concept. At its ftti_and_timing_budget.arithmetic_check statement it asserts: 'FB2-SAF-SGO-000001 now records the 15 ms margin as well, so the two records agree and the safety goal's budget closes ... and FB2-SAF-FSR-000003 now states those three points separately as 5 ms, 35 ms and 40 ms, so the requirement and this allocation agree.' That is a quantitative claim that a fault-tolerant time budget closes with 15 ms of margin. Checked against the two candidates: the synthetic_reference copy of FB2-SAF-FSR-000003 does carry the 40 ms figure, so the sentence is TRUE of the copy the corpus means. The as_is copy of the same identifier mentions neither 35 ms nor 40 ms, so the sentence is FALSE of it. Rename the synthetic side and this safety-budget closure argument silently comes to rest on a record that does not support it, with no validator output. The same applies to FB2-SAF-SGO-000001, whose two copies hold different safe-state sets - two conditions in as_is, four in synthetic_reference - and which this record already instructs must not be merged, at VOC-AMB-002, because merging would put a vehicle-level claim into a record describing a battery monitoring unit.",
   "why_this_is_not_simply_a_preference": "The corpus holds two committed positions on the same question and they contradict each other. The task framing for this pass names ID-RULE-003 as the sanctioned instrument. Both cannot govern. Choosing between them is a governance decision about which policy rule governs identifier collisions, and it should be recorded as one in corpus-policy.json rather than settled implicitly by whichever pass ran last.    "what_was_settled": "The shape is now fixed by record type in the schema that governs each type, so a consumer no longer has to know the convention to read the field. safety_concept.schema.json already constrained the concept side: `safety_strategies.fault_reaction` is an array with minItems 1 and every entry requires reaction, triggered_by, an element_id matching ^AR-[0-9]{3}$ and reaction_time_budget_ms. requirement.schema.json now declares the requirement side as a single object whose required core - reaction, triggered_by, allocated_element_id, element_owns_reaction, allocation_basis, mode_dependence, open_limits - is byte-for-byte the core all nine requirement records already carry.    "what_was_not_changed": "No record moved a reaction and no record changed shape. ### C542-std - standards_mapping

**Assertion.** This record maps to ISO_26262_2018 Part 1, Clause 4 with status `mapped` on the grounds: The vocabulary of terms the other parts of the standard introduce. This record supplies the reading of those terms AS THIS CORPUS USES THEM, which is what the corpus needed and did not have. No clause text is reproduced or paraphrased; the clause identifier is the whole of the standard reference.

- *Machine state:* no machine check: clause selection is not verifiable from the repository
- *Still needs a human:* Whether that clause is the right obligation for this work product and whether `mapped` is the right status.
- *Where to look:* The record verbatim in section 3.

### C543-std - standards_mapping

**Assertion.** This record maps to ISO_26262_2018 Part 1, Clause 5 with status `partially_mapped` on the grounds: The abbreviated terms the corpus uses (ASIL, FTTI, QM) and their expansions. The corpus uses all three abbreviations and defines none of them in a record; the expansions this record gives are the expansions the corpus's own prose and field names use, not a definition taken from the standard.

- *Machine state:* no machine check: clause selection is not verifiable from the repository

## 5. What is ALREADY checked, and by what

## 8. What your signature changes, and exactly what to write

Filling in section 9 is the only thing that changes `human_approval_status` on this record. It is currently `pending`. No automated process may fill it, and none can.

### 8.1 The rule that will read your signature

As of **2026-10-04** this is an EVIDENCE requirement, not a prohibition. The corpus used to run a rule that failed validation on any record whose `human_approval_status` was `approved`, however well evidenced - a ban, which cannot tell a fabricated approval from a real one because it never looks at one. That ban was replaced (amendment `APPROVAL-RULE-A1`, recorded at `docs/artifacts/governance/role-and-review-policy.json#/approval_evidence_contract`, whose text is kept there for the audit trail and whose element 6 has since been superseded). **Recording the first real approval no longer turns `corpus.py check` red.** What it does instead is make the tool check six things, and fail if any one is missing.

The corpus now reads its approval contract from `docs/artifacts/governance/role-and-review-policy.json#/approval_ledger_contract` (amendment `APPROVAL-LEDGER-A1`), which supersedes element 6 of the six-element contract and tightens element 5. Elements 1-4 and the production-authority bar are unchanged.

**A properly formed approval must carry all six of these:**

| # | element | what the validator actually checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the grant value | `human_approval_status` is `"approved"` (or `"rejected"` - both are recorded human decisions and both need a person behind them). A value on its own is necessary and **not sufficient**. |
| 2 | `approved_by` | a named individual, not a role and not a team. Rejected if it is a single token, if it equals a declared `role_id` or role name, if any token is a declared `role_id`, or if any token is in the team vocabulary (team, group, board, committee, panel, crew, squad, staff, department, automation, system, tool, agent, ...). |
| 3 | `role` + `independence` | `role` must be a `role_id` declared in `role-and-review-policy.json#/roles`. `independence` must be an object carrying `owner_role` (**must equal this record's own `owner_role`, which is `'safety_engineer'`**), `satisfied: true`, an `evidence` string of at least 24 characters that is not a placeholder, and a `policy_ref` naming `role-and-review-policy.json`. Then independence is ENFORCED, not just asserted: your role must differ from `safety_engineer` **and** from the author of the last `revision_history` entry that changed this record's content. |
| 4 | `date` | ISO-8601, `YYYY-MM-DD` optionally followed by `THH:MM[:SS]` and `Z` or an offset. Checked by grammar AND by parse. |
| 5 | `review_packet` | an object carrying `path`, `sha256` and `record_sha256_at_signing`. See 8.2 - this is the part reviewers get wrong. |
| 6 | `approval_ledger_ref` | an object naming your entry in the append-only ledger `docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl`: `ledger_id` plus `entry_sha256`. **Not** a `revision_history` entry - see 8.4 for why that matters more than it sounds. |

### 8.2 The packet digest, which is the part that is easy to get wrong

Three digests are involved and they are not interchangeable:

- `record_sha256_at_signing` is printed in section 4 of this packet and in this packet's `packet.json` under `integrity.record_sha256`. It is `beb85e09371508213f0e6d14dc2c353f19b88d8fb89c79263aca27fde35a0053`-class: the digest of THIS RECORD's bytes as they stand now. You can copy it straight out of section 4.
- `sha256` is the digest of **the archived signed packet you are citing** - the copy under `docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/` with your signature block filled in. It is not the digest of the generated packet in front of you: that is a different file, because yours has your signature in it. The packet cannot print its own digest, and it cannot print yours before you have written it. Do not type it. Let the generator resolve it:

```
python3 docs/artifacts/tools/make_review_packets.py --transcribe FB2-SAF-VOC-000001
```

  **Run it TWICE.** The first run tells you the signed-copy digest is NOT RESOLVED and to archive your signed packet first, because it cannot exist before you have signed. The second run, after the archived copy is on disk, resolves it from the file itself. The command writes nothing, appends nothing and fills no decision; it prints the exact `approval_evidence` block, the exact ledger entry and the exact `approval_ledger_ref` to merge, with your name, role, organisation and date left for you to supply.

What the validator does with them, so you can check your work:

1. `path` must be a `.json` packet twin under `docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/` and it must exist on disk. **A path under `docs/artifacts/reviews/packets/` is rejected**, with a message telling you to archive the signed packet first - and that rejection is correct: that tree is rewritten on every regeneration, so evidence left there does not survive. Nothing else outside `docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/` is admissible either.
2. `sha256` must equal that file's bytes **as they stand on disk now**. An archived signed packet is byte-stable by rule - it must not be edited after signing - so this digest keeps resolving. If you are regenerating packets for other records, your archived copy is untouched.
3. `record_sha256_at_signing` must equal **the packet's own** `integrity.record_sha256`. This is the binding that matters: citing a packet that exists, is the right shape and is byte-stable proves nothing unless its recorded record digest is the one you attested to. A digest belonging to a different record, a different revision, or a packet that was never on disk all fail here.
4. The cited packet must name THIS record in `target.record_id` **and** `target.profile` (the pair is the key under ID-RULE-004-A1), and its `integrity.record_path` must be this record's own file.

### 8.3 What happens to the numbers, read from the code

1. **The coverage dimension `human_approval` moves.** It used to be a literal 0/321 with the detail string "all artifacts pending human approval (none performed)" - a constant that measured nothing and would have read 0/321 after three hundred signatures. Since 2026-10-04 it is COMPUTED from the records, by the same predicate the validator enforces, so it reads 0/321 today and will read 1/321 the moment one properly evidenced, current approval is recorded. `production_authorization` is the same, with a STRICTLY higher bar: the approving role must be one the corpus grants production authority to (`architect` or `safety_manager`), and the record's family must be one human approval is required for (`safety_case`, `post_development_record`, `change`).
2. **Recording a properly formed approval keeps `corpus.py check` green.** The finding you would get for a bare `approved` names every unmet element, so if you get one, read it rather than guessing: it tells you which of the six is missing.
3. **`approval_staleness`, a counted metric, reports invalidated judgements.** It reads `stale / total approvals` on every coverage run and on `check`. If this record's content is corrected AFTER you approve it, your approval becomes STALE: that does not fail validation, but it is reported in a finding naming this record, your ledger entry and **which fields changed**, and it is excluded from the `human_approval` numerator. Re-review the changed fields and append a new ledger entry; do not edit or delete the old one.
4. **Two controls the signature does not touch.** `automated_review_status` describes machine checks, not your judgement - leave it alone. And the recursive key scan for authority claims (`production_release`, `authorized_for_production` and eight siblings, plus the ASIL/conformity/certification claim classes) is unchanged: nesting a production claim inside the new `approval_evidence` block is still caught.

### 8.4 How to record it, in order. Follow this order exactly.

1. **Fill section 9 in your own copy of this packet.** No tool may do it. No tool in this repository has a code path that writes a signature.
2. **Archive the signed packet** at `docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/<profile>/<id>.json`, keeping the twin byte-for-byte as you signed it. A corrected packet is a new document with a new signature, never an edit to a signed one. This archive is not optional and not advisory: it is the only place a signed packet is admissible from.
3. Run `--transcribe FB2-SAF-VOC-000001` and paste what it prints.
4. **A human appends the printed line to `docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl`** - one JSON object, one line, at the end. The ledger is append-only: entries are never reordered and never removed, and each entry names its predecessor's digest, so deleting or editing one breaks the chain and the validator reports where. The entry also carries `packet_first_commit`, the commit that first contained your archived packet; the validator confirms that commit exists and holds the blob.
5. Merge the printed `approval_ledger_ref` into the record, alongside `human_approval_status` and the `approval_evidence` block.

**Why there is no `revision_history` step, and why you must not add one.** An approval used to be recorded as a `revision_history` entry. A `revision_history` entry *is* a content change, so the record's `revision` has to move; a moved revision makes every link that pins that revision stale, and invalidates the `sha256` that every review record stores for the record. So an approval recorded that way breaks two controls nobody authorised breaking - which is why it was being recorded against the current revision as a workaround, which nobody had ratified. The ledger removes the conflict: an approval is an **event about** a record, not a change **to** it, and `approval_ledger_ref` is metadata excluded from the record's content digest. Recording your signature now costs nothing anywhere else. A self-test performs the whole recording on a throwaway copy of this tree and asserts that the revision does not move, no link goes stale and all 261 review digests still verify.

6. Run `python3 docs/artifacts/tools/corpus.py validate` and read the result. Zero approval findings means the approval is properly evidenced.

**What is still not yours to do, and what is still not provable.** Writing the approval value into the record needs a person: the gate now *accepts* a legitimately evidenced approval, which is what makes the guard meaningful, but *producing* one is a human act and the self-test `no record in the corpus carries an approval of any kind` fails the suite if one ever appears without a person.

And the limit worth knowing before you sign anything: **the hash chain proves existence, ordering and integrity, and the git anchor proves when and in what state your packet was committed. Neither proves that you read this record, and none of it makes your approval unforgeable.** A determined person can write all six elements, archive a packet, cite a real commit and maintain the chain correctly. That limit is irreducible. See `docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.md`.

`docs/artifacts/governance/closing-list.md` states what is still outstanding and who owns it. Read it before recording anything.
